Snap bar and screen edges get in the way of automatic tiling. So they run as two modes – switch between them with the shortcut or here.
Mode 1 – Snap bar and screen edges
Snap bar, screen edges, window magnet, shortcuts and swap windows.
Automatic tiling, swap windows, shortcuts, and the window magnet for floating windows.
Automatic tiling is switched off – only mode 1 runs and the mode shortcut does nothing.
Snap bar and screen edges are switched off – only mode 2 runs and the mode shortcut does nothing.
Click or press %1 to switch the mode.
Only one mode is switched on.
Every feature can be switched on and off on its own.
Drag a window to the top edge of the screen and drop it onto a zone.
Push a window against an edge or corner: maximize, halves, quarters.
Windows stick to each other and to the screen edges.
Snap the active window with key combinations.
Every window gets its place by itself, like in a tiling window manager.
Two windows trade places: drop one onto the other, or by key.
Shows where the window lands while a zone of the snap bar is highlighted. Off: no preview at all.
Shows where the window lands at an edge or corner. Off: no preview at all.
Show previews in the accent color
Off: a neutral frame – only for the previews that are switched on.
Pause KDE's edge tiling and its preview
Turn this off if you prefer KDE's own outline – then switch the screen edges preview above off.
Restore the original size when dragging a window out
KDE has its own screen edge actions and window snapping. When the same feature is on here, turn KDE's off: System Settings → Window Management → Screen Edges, and Window Behavior → Movement.
Colors, size and shape of the snap bar.
The default values are based on Windows 11.
Trigger distance from the top edge
Distance at which the handle appears
Active width along the top edge
Distance before the bar hides again
How far the bar slides down
Drag the cards to change the order in the snap bar. Double-click a card to edit it.
Push a window against an edge or a corner of the screen and it fills that part. Works with or without the snap bar.
Independent of the snap bar. Each edge can be switched on its own.
Left and right edge: half of the screen
Fit around windows that are already snapped
If a window sits at the bottom, the top edge gives the top half instead of maximizing. Halves and quarters also leave snapped windows uncovered.
How close the cursor has to get to the edge.
How long the window has to rest against the edge – a small push. 0 = at once.
Part of each side that counts as corner.
Hold at the edge to fill the free space
A short push gives the half or quarter. Keep the window at the edge a moment longer and it grows up to the next window – the preview shows it.
How long the window has to stay at the edge before it grows.

KDE's own maximize and tile at the screen edges – with its outline – pause while KSnapUnity runs, so only one preview appears. Your KDE settings are not changed: switch this off, disable or remove KSnapUnity and KDE's own behavior is back.
KDE's own screen edge actions are still on, so two helpers react to the same drag. Turn off “Maximize” and “Tile” in System Settings → Window Management → Screen Edges.
While you move or resize a window, its edges stick to nearby windows and to the screen edges.
Independent of the snap bar and the screen edges.
How close an edge has to come before it clicks into place.
A window stops at the edge of another one, also when you move it fast. Shake the mouse or keep pushing for a moment to let go. 0 = windows can overlap freely.
Windows stop at “Gap between windows” from the General page instead of touching.
When you resize a window, windows that touch it move their shared edge along – nothing overlaps, no gap opens.
Windows above each other keep their left and right edges together, windows side by side their top and bottom edges.
Shake the mouse quickly back and forth while resizing and the other windows jump back. A fast pull in one direction never lets go.
While resizing, windows that do not follow are shown transparent.
Pause KDE's snap zones while the magnet is on
So only one magnet pulls at a window. Your KDE settings are not changed: switch this off, disable or remove KSnapUnity and KDE's own snapping is back.
KDE's own window snapping is on as well. For one consistent feel, set its snap zones to “None” in System Settings → Window Management → Window Behavior → Movement.
Snap the active window with the keyboard. These are normal KDE global shortcuts – you also find them in System Settings → Shortcuts → KWin.
Off: the keys stay assigned but do nothing.
Sets the keys of all actions at once. You can still change single keys below.
Gives every action the key of the chosen scheme again and removes keys the scheme does not have.
KDE's shortcut service did not answer. You can still set the keys in System Settings → Shortcuts → KWin.
The snapping actions use the same gaps as the snap bar and remember the size before snapping: “Restore the size before snapping” brings it back.
K for KWin · Snap for snapping smarter · Unity for everything in one system
All window features in one system.
Grab a window by its title bar and drag it up. The snap bar slides down; drop the window onto a zone and it fills exactly that area. Drag it away again and it gets its old size back.
Snapping and automatic tiling run as two modes – one shortcut switches between them.
If you like KSnapUnity, you can support its development – thank you!
Every window gets its place on the screen by itself. New windows join in, closed ones leave room for the others.
Off: windows stay where you put them. The other features work either way.

Every layout you build on the Layouts page can arrange windows too – it appears above. Window 1 gets zone 1 and so on; more windows share the last zone. With fewer windows than zones “Main and stack” is used, so no holes appear.
Example: two windows side by side, from three on main and stack, from five a grid. Without a matching rule the layout chosen above is used.
Also changes when you resize the main window by hand.
How many windows share the main area (layout “Main and stack”).
Mirrors the layout: the main window sits on the right, the others on the left.
Less than 100 % keeps a lone window centered – nice on wide screens.
A lone window uses the whole screen, even when a margin is set.
When a window opens, closes or swaps, the others move smoothly instead of jumping.
These applications are never arranged and keep their own place. Dialogs always float.
Open the application first, then pick it here.
Drag a window onto another one to swap them. Drop it on the snap bar or a screen edge and it floats freely; “Float the window” brings it back. Gaps come from the General page.
Two windows trade places – drop one onto the other, or use the keys.
Main switch for dragging and the keys.
Drop a window onto another one
Drag a window over the middle of another one – the preview shows two arrows – and let go. With automatic tiling anywhere over the other window will do.
Change them on the Keyboard shortcuts page. With automatic tiling, the windows also trade their places in the order.
Your own layouts and their order will be lost.
